title: A Preregistered Audit of Dataset Contamination Controls in LLM-for-NetOps Benchmarks (Revised)
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory audit to assess whether conservative deterministic contamination detectors (exact normalized equality + fuzzy 5‑gram + provenance heuristics) flag items in a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample and whether applying preregistered guarded exclusions changes validator‑measured success rates. The executed run used provenance‑stable synthetic tasks produced by a deterministic generator and shared‑generation semantics (one model call per item reused across baseline and guarded conditions). Consequently the prespecified primary confirmatory hypothesis (H2: paired success‑rate decrease after guarded exclusions) was rendered uninformative for detecting generation‑level contamination in this execution: all 150 baseline and 150 guarded episodes passed the deterministic oracle (baseline = 150/150, guarded = 150/150), giving a paired difference = 0.0 percentage points (95% CI [0.0,0.0]); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. We explicitly declare and document the preregistration→execution deviation (planned public datasets → executed synthetic sampling) and the execution semantics that produced this degenerate outcome, cite the archived artifacts that substantiate each point, and recommend concrete artifact‑anchored design changes—independent per‑condition generation, provenance‑rich public sampling, always‑persisted per‑item overlap scores, and multi‑model replication—to make future audits sensitive to public‑corpus contamination.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs are being evaluated and proposed for operational NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation and automated configuration repair. Such evaluations drive operational trust decisions, so measurement validity matters: performance inflated by dataset contamination (items or templates appearing in model training corpora) undermines trust. Recent surveys and benchmarks have therefore recommended contamination detection (token‑fingerprinting, n‑gram overlap, provenance tracing) and validator‑backed oracles for functional correctness. We preregistered a confirmatory audit to test whether a conservative, deterministic detector suite would (a) flag a non‑zero fraction of sampled NetOps items and (b) produce a measurable paired drop in validator pass rates when high‑confidence flagged items are excluded and deterministically replaced. The preregistration (study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1) froze detectors, exclusion rules, estimands, sampling, and analysis before execution. The executed run produced artifact‑verifiable numbers (complete_pair_count = 150, baseline_success_count = 150, guarded_success_count = 150) but, crucially, was degenerate for the prespecified confirmatory test because the executed sampling and generation semantics differed from the sampling regime implied by parts of the preregistration. This paper revises the original manuscript to (1) explicitly record that deviation with artifact citations, (2) reclassify the primary confirmatory hypothesis as untestable/degenerate under the executed semantics while nonetheless reporting the exact archived outcomes, and (3) provide artifact‑anchored recommendations for future audits that would be sensitive to contamination in web‑sourced benchmarks.
sections.related_work: Prior work shows that LLMs can produce plausible NetOps configurations and that integrate–verify patterns (generate→validate→repair) increase average repair reliability. Benchmark and system papers (e.g., recent evaluations of agentic repair and generate‑verify pipelines) demonstrate promise but also highlight per‑case regressions and dependence on dataset construction and oracles. Metaresearch and survey literature warn that benchmark contamination and construct invalidity (templated tasks) can inflate measured accuracy; recommended defenses include deterministic fingerprinting, fuzzy n‑gram overlap, provenance timestamps, and transparent detector reporting. Our study implements a conservative subset of those defenses in a fully preregistered pipeline and focuses on the operational question: do those defenses change validator outcomes under a reproducible sampling and generation regime? Unlike capability leaderboards, our contribution is a preregistered audit with full execution artifacts and an explicit preregistration→execution reconciliation.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary estimand. The preregistration (contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1) specified the primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (H2), exact McNemar two‑sided primary test, and a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). The preregistered benchmark_scope listed four public datasets (OpenAlex IDs: https://openalex.org/W7157506260, https://openalex.org/W4404602270, https://openalex.org/W4404534210, https://openalex.org/W7166900660) and a deterministic synthetic option. Sampling plan: task_count = 150 confirmatory items (planned 50 per dataset when available) and paired evaluation across baseline vs guarded conditions, with deterministic replacement rules for excluded items.

Execution choices and explicit preregistration→execution deviation. The archived execution artifacts show that the confirmatory sample used provenance‑stable synthetic tasks (each task_manifest entry uses source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and that the pipeline executed with shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation = false) so a single model generation per item was reused for both baseline and guarded episodes unless a high‑confidence flag triggered replacement. These executed facts are documented in the archived artifacts: execution/task_manifest.jsonl (sha256: b7c08599e3f96d8d5605a18f8f973e0707d7224327eeed7bde78c0d34cb83e55) and execution/model_configuration.json (sha256: a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). The preregistration→execution mismatch is therefore a substantive deviation: the preregistered sampling_plan allowed (and originally described) sampling public datasets but the executed confirmatory run sampled synthetic provenance‑stable items. We explicitly record this deviation here and cite the archived artifacts; this is not a retrospective change of estimand but a required disclosure of execution facts that render the primary confirmatory test uninformative for detecting public‑benchmarks leakage in this run.

Contamination detector implementation and persistence policy. The preregistered detector suite implemented: (1) exact normalized token equality; (2) fuzzy 5‑gram shingle overlap with preregistered high‑confidence threshold ≥ 0.80 (medium thresholds at 0.65 and 0.50 for sensitivity analyses); and (3) provenance timestamp heuristics. The detector workflow persisted detailed per‑item fuzzy overlap outputs only when thresholds were crossed or replacements were invoked (this implementation choice and its path are recorded in the transformation manifest: execution/transformation_manifest.json; see execution manifest). Because no high‑confidence flags occurred in the run, the pipeline did not persist a complete global per‑item overlap table—an artifact‑grounded absence we document and discuss below. The detector persistence policy is recorded in the archived transformation manifest and is the reason analysis/contamination_summary.csv (sha256: 389227f0d1e81239c7498abd4944a04c59c92c5fa042b990e332796cd61c3222) contains no flagged rows rather than a table of all overlap scores.

Generation semantics and verifier. The declared model was gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json) and the deterministic validator was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0). The validator applies a parse→state_update simulation and enforces the preregistered full_intent_constraint_validation rule (final modeled state matches expected_final_state on allowed fields and workflow constraints are respected). The validator emits binary pass/fail and archived traces per episode (parsing counts, observed_touched_field_count, violation_codes). All validator traces and raw responses are archived under execution/raw_results.jsonl (sha256: 5337998d1d86aca507f77659d75cc9487cf3d87a157ed5044b8a9d5ff79b5586) and per‑episode scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/*.json).
sections.results:
Execution accounting and deterministic reconciliation. The run completed planned_episode_count = 300 (150 item pairs) with completed_episode_count = 300 and failed_episode_count = 0; provider accounting shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 150 because each item used a shared initial generation (model_calls_used = 150) under independent_condition_generation = false. These counts and reconciliation checks are recorded in the execution manifest and deterministic_reconciliation artifact (see execution manifest representative_artifact_hashes).

Contamination detector outputs. The preregistered detectors produced zero high‑confidence contamination flags for the executed sample: analysis/contamination_summary.csv contains no flagged rows. Because the detector persisted detailed overlap outputs only on threshold crossings or replacement events, no global per‑item overlap distribution is present in the archive for this run; this absence is an explicit consequence of the recorded detector persistence policy (transformation manifest path in execution manifest).

Validator outcomes and primary estimand numbers. The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 passed all baseline episodes (baseline_success_count = 150/150; baseline_success_rate = 1.0) and all guarded episodes (guarded_success_count = 150/150; guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n11 = 150, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The observed paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline = 0.0 percentage points. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. These numbers are artifact‑grounded in analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (sha256: c2ba9cdb5d0938eae910129ba511eadf309319e6e05b36d9e3b4860032deb80e).

Representative diagnostic episode. Representative archived episode pair-000001 shows identical normalized_reference_answer and normalized_response and a validator trace with parsed_command_count = required_command_count = 4 and score = VALID_CONFIGURATION. The per‑episode JSON and response files are archived (examples in execution/responses and execution/scoring with listed hashes) and substantiate the validator behavior described above.

Formal reclassification of the primary confirmatory test. Because independent_condition_generation = false and no high‑confidence exclusions occurred, baseline and guarded outputs were identical by construction (a single shared generation per item was reused). Therefore, the preregistered primary confirmatory test H2 (a paired drop in success rate after guarded exclusions) is untestable/degenerate in this executed configuration: the observed n11 = 150 concordance is an artifact‑driven diagnostic outcome rather than substantive evidence that contamination is absent in web‑sourced public benchmarks. We report the exact archived statistics above but explicitly reclassify H2 as uninformative for the originally intended question about public dataset contamination under this run. This formal reclassification and the artifacts that motivate it (execution/task_manifest.jsonl sha256: b7c08599..., execution/model_configuration.json sha256: a40e96e2...) are recorded here.
sections.discussion:
Why the run was degenerate (artifact‑anchored). Two execution facts recorded in the archive jointly explain the degenerate paired outcome: (1) the sampled items were provenance‑stable synthetic tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5, and (2) the pipeline reused a single model generation per item across baseline and guarded conditions (independent_condition_generation = false). Both facts are visible in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and execution/model_configuration.json and cause identical baseline vs guarded outputs whenever no guarded exclusion occurs; this logically forces n10 = n01 = 0 and makes the paired test incapable of revealing generation‑level contamination.

Implications of detector persistence policy and missing overlap table. The detector implementation persisted detailed fuzzy overlap outputs only when threshold crossings or replacements occurred (documented in execution/transformation_manifest.json). Consequently, because no items met the high‑confidence threshold, the archive contains no global per‑item overlap distribution. This absence constrains post‑hoc interpretability: readers cannot inspect how close any item was to being flagged (e.g., maximum overlaps). The remedy is straightforward and artifact‑anchored: persist all per‑item overlap scores regardless of threshold crossing so future audits can report min/median/max overlap statistics and perform sensitivity analyses; this change is implementable without changing detector logic.

Design changes to make future audits sensitive to public‑corpus contamination. The archived run supports concrete recommendations: (a) sample provenance‑rich public items (URLs/DOIs/timestamps) instead of synthetic items when the question targets public‑corpus contamination; (b) set independent_condition_generation = true to ensure baseline and guarded outputs are independently realized per item (recordable in execution/model_configuration.json) so generation‑level discordance can occur; (c) always persist per‑item fuzzy overlap scores (analysis/contamination_scores.csv) to enable threshold‑sensitivity reporting; (d) expand to multi‑model and multi‑seed designs to raise expected discordance rates and statistical power; and (e) add paraphrase‑robust detectors and human adjudication for borderline cases. Each recommendation directly follows from the recorded gaps in the archived artifacts (model_calls_used = 150 vs planned_maximum_model_calls = 300, empty contamination_summary.csv, lack of overlap table) and is implementable within the same execution framework.

Practical caution on inference. The artifact‑verified result only supports the narrow inference that, under provenance‑stable synthetic sampling and shared generation semantics, the conservative detectors did not flag high‑confidence contamination and the guarded policy performed no replacements. It does not imply absence of contamination in web‑sourced benchmarks nor failure of the preregistered detectors in other sampling regimes.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑archived paired audit of conservative contamination detectors for LLM‑for‑NetOps evaluation. The run yielded zero high‑confidence flags and identical validator pass rates (150/150 baseline and guarded) because synthetic provenance sampling and shared per‑item generation semantics collapsed baseline vs guarded discordance. We explicitly record this preregistration→execution deviation and formally reclassify the prespecified primary confirmatory test as uninformative for the original public‑benchmark contamination question under the executed configuration. We report exact archived numbers and traces, and we recommend concrete artifact‑anchored design changes—provenance‑rich public sampling, independent per‑condition generation, always‑persisted per‑item overlap scores, and multi‑model replication—to make future preregistered audits sensitive to contamination in web‑sourced benchmarks. All artifacts and validator traces cited above are archived and available in the execution bundle as indicated in the Disclosure Statement below.

The execution followed the preregistered missingness, retry, and exclusion policies; no deviations other than the documented sampling choice (synthetic tasks) and shared generation semantics occurred.
limitations: Single‑model execution (gpt‑5-mini) — results do not generalize across other LLM families, sizes, or training corpora.

The executed confirmatory sample used provenance‑stable synthetic/deterministically generated tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:"); absence of high‑confidence flags here does not imply absence of contamination in real‑world, web‑crawled benchmarks.

Generation semantics used shared_initial_candidate across baseline and guarded conditions (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical outputs when no exclusions occurred and thus limiting sensitivity to the intended paired intervention.

Contamination detection relied on preregistered conservative lexical heuristics (exact match and fuzzy 5‑gram overlap thresholds); paraphrased memorization and subtler leakage patterns may escape these heuristics and require paraphrase‑robust detectors and human adjudication.

Passing the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 indicates satisfaction of the checked functional constraints but does not imply comprehensive production readiness or absence of semantic regressions outside the validator's modeled scope.
